sources.admitted_role: Public basis for the aiming quasimode: a quasimode is a mode that exists only while a person actively holds a control down (a shift key, a trigger, a button), and reverts automatically the instant the control is released, which grounds the family's aiming phase as a state that exists only while a session is live and the aiming hand is holding it, rather than a persistent toggled mode
admitted_claims: A quasimode is defined as a mode a system remains in only as long as a person continuously holds a designated control, distinct from a mode that is switched on and stays on until switched off again

The quasimode concept is presented as a way to avoid the mode-confusion cost of a persistent mode switch, because releasing the held control always and unambiguously returns the system to its base state

The quasimode's held control is a single physical input the person cannot mistake for being active or inactive, which the article ties to reducing the class of error where a person forgets which mode a system is in
excluded_uses: No specific device, key binding, or product example is depended upon; only the held-control-defines-the-mode's-lifetime concept informs the aiming phase and the sticky aiming-hand rule
No claim that this family's aiming phase eliminates mode confusion or reads as intended without a Device Lab or usability receipt

sources.admitted_role: Public basis for the mode-error literature the aiming quasimode answers: a mode error occurs when a person's action is correct for the mode they believe is active but the system is actually in a different mode, which grounds the family's decision to make the aiming phase visible only through the ghost preview and to end it deterministically on commit or cancel rather than leaving an ambiguous residual state
admitted_claims: A mode error happens when a system's response to the same input differs depending on hidden or ambiguous internal state, and no visible signal disambiguates which state the system is in at the time of the action
A system that resolves an action through a single, visibly indicated state is documented as less prone to mode errors than one whose state is implicit or inferred from history

The literature recommends making an active mode continuously visible for as long as it is active, and ending it through an explicit, unambiguous action rather than a timeout or an incidental side effect
excluded_uses: No mode-error mitigation technique or interface pattern is copied; only the general finding that hidden or ambiguous state invites mode errors informs the closed placement-phase set and its deterministic transitions
No claim that this family's phase model eliminates mode errors without a Device Lab or usability receipt
